title: I Took the Marimba-Bar Checkout to the Percussion Lead Who Left My Numbered Set

parts.text: I stepped into the percussion bay at 4:07 p.m. and lead Oren was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE SET. NINETY MINUTES. BARS STAY WITH THE CHECKOUT. I was thirty, section secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered bars. Oren shrugged. "Leads are the bars." I photographed the board, the booking, and his leftover mallets on my numbered set. Then I asked for the bar log. At 4:15 the cage pinged why Oren's name was on my rosewood. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The cage can see Oren's leftover mallets on my numbered set.

social.video_title: He left my numbered marimba bars on my checkout — Part 1/2
social.description: Percussion bay, leftover mallets, a ninety-minute clock he posted. I logged the rosewood. Would you have asked for the bar log?

parts.text: Oren called it roll practice until the cage asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the mallet still. The bars went back to my numbered checkout. Oren ran a slot of his own and told the next lead atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: LEADS ARE NOT THE BARS. I keep my set on a labeled rack. Oren brown-bags his rolls. The bay finally looks like a checkout, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Leads are not the bars — Part 2/2
social.description: Bar log, numbered set, and a second line on the board. Was roll practice ever my rosewood?
